title: What If Earth Stopped Spinning for 1 Second?
next_video: What If You Fell Into Jupiter?
voice_style: curious, warm, precise; mid-pace; slight pause before every reveal

beats.text: Right now, Earth's spin carries you at up to {{v_eq_kmh}} kilometers per hour, and you can't feel it.
So what if, for one second, the ground under you stopped, and everything else didn't?
Welcome to The If Engine, where we run impossible scenarios through real physics, and show you the math.

First, the speed. Earth turns once every {{sidereal_h}} hours relative to the stars. That's the sidereal day, about four minutes shorter than the 24-hour day on your clock, because Earth is also circling the Sun.
Divide the distance around the equator by that time, and you get about {{v_eq_ms}} meters per second. That's roughly {{v_eq_kmh}} kilometers per hour, faster than the speed of sound.
But not everyone moves that fast. The farther you are from the equator, the smaller the circle you trace every day.

In Singapore, you're doing about {{v_singapore_ms}} meters per second. In Cairo, {{v_cairo_ms}}. New York, {{v_newyork_ms}}. London, {{v_london_ms}}. And at the North Pole, you're just turning in place.
We never feel any of this, because the ground, the air, the oceans and you are all moving together, at a steady speed. Motion you share with everything around you is motion you can't feel.
beats.kinetic: Moving together = feels like standing still

beats.text: Which is exactly why breaking that agreement, even for one second, is such a terrible idea.
Here are the rules of today's experiment.

beats.text: Rule one: the solid Earth, every rock and everything bolted to it, stops rotating instantly.

beats.text: Rule two: it stays perfectly still for exactly one second.

beats.text: Everything that isn't rock, the air, the water, and you, simply follows Newton's first law. It keeps moving at the speed it already had.

It snaps back to its normal spin

visual.caption: Air, water and people keep the velocity they had

beats.text: Let's start the clock. At time zero, the ground stops. Say you're standing on the equator. From the ground's point of view, you're suddenly hurtling east at {{v_eq_ms}} meters per second.

Can friction save you? Rubber on dry concrete can slow you down at about {{friction_decel}} meters per second squared. Over the whole second, that takes off just {{friction_dv}} meters per second. You'd still be going {{v_after_friction}}.
If nothing were in your way, you'd tumble almost half a kilometer in that one second.
But on a planet covered in walls, trees and cars, something is always in your way. So how hard is that hit?
beats.retention: Open loop: how hard is the hit?

beats.text: At {{v_eq_ms}} meters per second, a {{person_mass}} kilogram person carries about {{ke_person_mj}} megajoules of kinetic energy. That's the energy released by roughly {{ke_person_tnt}} kilograms of TNT.
Here's another way to feel that number. Hitting a wall at that speed is like falling from a height of {{fall_height_km}} kilometers, with no air to slow you down. That's higher than Mount Everest.
In London, the numbers are smaller, but not small enough. Even at {{v_london_ms}} meters per second, it's the same as falling from {{fall_height_london_km}} kilometers.
Now, buildings. Unlike you, they're anchored to the rock. So when the rock stops, their foundations stop with it, instantly.
The upper floors don't know that yet. The news travels up the structure as a shear wave, a kind of sound wave in steel, moving at about {{c_steel}} meters per second.
The stress that wave carries is density, times wave speed, times the sudden change in velocity. For steel, that's about {{steel_stress_gpa}} gigapascals.

Common structural steel starts to give way in shear at around {{steel_yield_mpa}} megapascals. Our stress wave is about {{steel_ratio}} times that. Structures bolted to the ground just aren't built for a jolt like this.
And yet, as bad as all that is, it isn't the biggest problem. The biggest problem is the thing you can't see.
The atmosphere isn't bolted to anything. When the ground stops, the air keeps going. At the equator, that's a wind of {{v_eq_ms}} meters per second, blowing from west to east.

At sea level, sound travels at about {{c_air}} meters per second. So at the equator, this wind is Mach {{mach}}. It stays supersonic everywhere within about {{supersonic_lat}} degrees of the equator. That's {{supersonic_area_frac}} of Earth's surface, all at once.

Anything standing in its way gets pushed with at least half the air density times the wind speed squared. That's {{q_kpa}} kilopascals, about {{q_tonnes}} tonnes of force on every square meter of wall.

For comparison, a Category 5 hurricane starts at {{cat5_kmh}} kilometers per hour. That push grows with the square of the speed, so our wind pushes about {{hurricane_ratio}} times harder than the minimum Category 5 wind.
Across that zone, every building, tree and hill would grow its own shock wave. Picture a sonic boom, but instead of one passing jet, it comes from every obstacle at the same moment.
Altogether, the moving air carries about {{atm_ke}} joules of kinetic energy relative to the ground. That's roughly {{atm_ke_years}} years of humanity's entire energy use.

But here's the twist. It only has one second to deliver it. In one second, even the fastest air moves less than half a kilometer, and most of the air above the rooftops never touches anything solid before the ground starts again.

Now, the oceans. Like the air, the water keeps moving while the sea floor stops. The open ocean is, on average, {{ocean_depth_km}} kilometers deep, and near the equator that entire column of water slides east by up to {{one_sec_distance}} meters.
That's about {{ocean_volume_per_m}} million cubic meters of water shoved toward the shore for every single meter of coastline in its path. Roughly {{olympic_pools}} Olympic swimming pools, per meter.

But the coasts are where it gets violent. When fast-moving water slams into a steep rock face, it can't get out of the way. Engineers call this water hammer, and the pressure spike is density, times the speed of sound in water, times the impact speed.
With water hitting rock at {{v_eq_ms}} meters per second, that's around {{hammer_mpa}} megapascals, more than {{hammer_ratio_floor}} times the crushing pressure at the bottom of the Mariana Trench.
On the coasts facing the other way, the water does the reverse. It pulls away from the land, for a moment uncovering the sea floor near the shore.

Once the ground starts again, gravity tries to level everything out, and that sends tsunamis across every ocean. In water {{ocean_depth_km}} kilometers deep, a tsunami travels at about {{tsunami_kmh}} kilometers per hour, nearly as fast as a jet airliner, crossing {{ocean_cross_km}} kilometers of ocean in about {{ocean_cross_h}} hours.

How tall would those waves be? Honestly, that depends on the shape of every coastline and sea floor. That takes a supercomputer, not a video. But the push is enormous, and it reaches every ocean basin at once.
So, is anyone safe? Surprisingly, yes. Anyone who isn't touching the ground.
A cruising airliner is carried by the air around it, and that air doesn't stop. For that one second, passengers would feel nothing at all, while the ground far below them lurches to a halt.

And the astronauts on the International Space Station, orbiting at about {{iss_kmh}} kilometers per hour, wouldn't notice anything. Their orbit doesn't care how fast the planet underneath is spinning.
Then the second is up. The rock snaps back to full speed.

That should fix everything, right? Not quite. Anything that got slowed down during that second, by hitting a wall, scraping along the ground or piling up against a coast, is now moving slower than the ground again.
beats.retention: Reversal: the fix makes it worse

beats.text: So the jolt happens again, in reverse. Everything that was stopped gets hit by the restarting planet at up to {{v_eq_ms}} meters per second, from the other direction.
Two hits, one second apart. That's the real price of a single stopped second.
Once the dust settles, there's one strange, permanent change. Earth has lost exactly one second of rotation.
In that second, the planet should have turned by about {{rot_arcsec}} arcseconds. It didn't. So every place on Earth is now one second behind where the stars say it should be.

Astronomers track exactly this kind of drift. Atomic clocks keep steady time, but Earth's spin isn't perfectly steady, so since 1972, timekeepers have inserted {{leap_count}} leap seconds to keep our clocks in step with the planet.
So after all that destruction, the official cleanup would include one tiny line item: one more leap second.

So, what if Earth stopped spinning for one second? A supersonic wind, a stress wave through every building, water hammer on the coasts, tsunamis in every ocean, and then the whole thing again in reverse.
One second is short. Momentum doesn't care.
Every number in this video comes from a calculation or a cited source, and the sources are in the description, so go ahead and check our math.

Next time, we leave solid ground behind entirely. What happens if you fall into Jupiter, a planet with no solid surface to land on? Subscribe so you don't miss it. This was The If Engine. Run the impossible. Do the math.

metadata.summary: We run the scenario through real physics and show every calculation on screen: the supersonic wind, the shear wave through every building, water hammer on the coasts, ocean-wide tsunamis, the restart, and the one permanent change (Earth ends up exactly one second late).
key_numbers: Wind if the ground stops: Mach {{mach}}, ram pressure ≥ {{q_kpa}} kPa (≈ {{hurricane_ratio}}× a minimum Cat-5 wind)

metadata.assumptions: Assumptions: the solid Earth stops instantly, holds for exactly 1 s, then resumes. Wave heights are not estimated (they need coastline-resolving simulations).
